chapter: Critics and the thinning Chicago scene (draft typing)
title: Chicago 1931-38: the Depression, radio, accordions and show business
summary: Hodes says people first listened as an audience in New York in 1938, not Chicago. In Chicago he describes the lean years, with accordions, radio and the Depression pushing small bands out and agents demanding extra acts. They also touch on Louis Armstrong's struggles.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Well, when did people start coming to hear the music? When did the music become public? We talked earlier about the bands being sort of functional, what went on --
I didn't see it until I got to New York, in '38. I saw it in the Hickory House.
But not in Chicago.
No. Buddy Rich on drums and Joe Marsala at the band, and that's where I saw it.
Yeah. Well, what happened between '31 and '38 in Chicago?
You tried to live those years without eating. That was when the accordion came into being. That was when you went up to see an agent and you said, I got a

little band, and the guys says, what else do you do? Do you wear funny hats? Do you have a dance routine? Do you go around the tables? Do you have some songs? What else do you do? And it had become not enough that you had a band to play music. You had to do something else.
Be in show business.
Show business. And it became a -- that came with the accordion. The accordion came in and the accordion was an instrument that you could go from table to table and play. And play music.
Is there an accordion on one side of that record?
I think there may be on that thing. I think the piano player that day, or somebody sold him on the idea of using it.
I thought you were on the date, too.
No, no.
You weren't on the date with him.
The only date I made with him was the So, little by little, the music was going out the window. Just all sorts of explanations. Radio was coming in.
And the Depression came, too.
And the Depression. And with radio, big bands sound good on radio, little bands don't sound so

good. So they stopped. The big band with the (inaudible). And so we were slowly -- and Louis Armstrong wasn't -- tried doing it by himself and he has having a hard time. I think Red Saunders taught us a little about the hard time that he had trying even to put a hall together and rent a hall and do something to keep his way of life.
Work became very scarce.
Yeah. Well, Louis had gone on the road with Zilner Randolph. Well, he had gone to New York.
Come back.
And Zilner Randolph put together a band and they had a tour of the South.
